messages.subject: Can I use INLA when I do not have original SPDE?
parts:
To whom it may concern,

I am a green hand to INLA and I have quick questions on it. When I deal with nested spde model (the equation for it shown below), the basis function can be represented as w=Hv, and w does not have markov property. Is that possible for me to use INLA when I define a new Q matrix in rgeneric function that Q=HQ0H, where H and Q0 are sparse and Q0 is the precision matrix for a GMRF v?  If so, what is the hyperparameters stand for? In my understanding, for a typical SPDE,  we will have precision for observations, range and stdev. In my case, we will have precision for observations, theta1 and theta2. Here, dose theta1 still has the relationship with log(range) and theta2 is connected with log(kappa)?

yours,
Yimeng Wang

parts:
In that model, the amount (and direction) of anisotropy would be controlled by B, and the range in the direction orthogonal to B is determined by \kappa. The standard deviation will be decided by a combination of all three parameters (see Example 2 in the original nested SPDE paper). 

Note that you would have precision matrix H^-1 Q0 H^{-T}, where Q0 and H are sparse. So if you implement it in rgeneric you would need to merge H with the A matrix to get a sparse approximation. In this case, you need to assume that the parameters of H are fixed, since the A matrix is not allowed to depend on parameters in R-INLA. 

There is some (very old) code for defining and sampling models like this based on R-INLA functions here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T3nK8D7wengCT_A9jVIbZGSoVm9R4UDz/view

messages.author: 2a6271869edfdebb
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can I use INLA when I do not have original SPDE?
parts:
The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau. 

Regarding the second question, since the model is not Markov, the trick is to realize that you can write X ~ N(0, (H^-1 Q0 H^{-T})^{-1}) as X =  H w0, where w0 ~ N(0,Q0^{-1}), so w0 is the latent GMRF that would be used in INLA. Then if you have the likelihood Y = AX + e for example, this is Y= AHw0 + e, so that AH would be the "observation matrix" for the latent  field w0. 

-David

The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau.

Yes, that is correct. Unless you merge A and H, you need to use the dense matrix Q=H^-1 Q0 H^{-T} as precision, which will be very slow. If you treat H as fixed, then you should indeed be able to just use A %*% H in the stack for the standard spde model.

On Wed, Apr 5, 2023 at 12:09 PM David Bolin <da...@r-inla.org> wrote:
The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau. 

Regarding the second question, since the model is not Markov, the trick is to realize that you can write X ~ N(0, (H^-1 Q0 H^{-T})^{-1}) as X =  H w0, where w0 ~ N(0,Q0^{-1}), so w0 is the latent GMRF that would be used in INLA. Then if you have the likelihood Y = AX + e for example, this is Y= AHw0 + e, so that AH would be the "observation matrix" for the latent  field w0. 

-David

Yimeng Wang

On Tue, Apr 4, 2023 at 3:00 PM David Bolin <da...@r-inla.org> wrote:
In that model, the amount (and direction) of anisotropy would be controlled by B, and the range in the direction orthogonal to B is determined by \kappa. The standard deviation will be decided by a combination of all three parameters (see Example 2 in the original nested SPDE paper). 

Note that you would have precision matrix H^-1 Q0 H^{-T}, where Q0 and H are sparse. So if you implement it in rgeneric you would need to merge H with the A matrix to get a sparse approximation. The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau. 

Regarding the second question, since the model is not Markov, the trick is to realize that you can write X ~ N(0, (H^-1 Q0 H^{-T})^{-1}) as X =  H w0, where w0 ~ N(0,Q0^{-1}), so w0 is the latent GMRF that would be used in INLA. Then if you have the likelihood Y = AX + e for example, this is Y= AHw0 + e, so that AH would be the "observation matrix" for the latent  field w0. 

-David

In that model, the amount (and direction) of anisotropy would be controlled by B, and the range in the direction orthogonal to B is determined by \kappa. The standard deviation will be decided by a combination of all three parameters (see Example 2 in the original nested SPDE paper). 

Note that you would have precision matrix H^-1 Q0 H^{-T}, where Q0 and H are sparse. So if you implement it in rgeneric you would need to merge H with the A matrix to get a sparse approximation. In this case, you need to assume that the parameters of H are fixed, since the A matrix is not allowed to depend on parameters in R-INLA. 

There is some (very old) code for defining and sampling models like this based on R-INLA functions here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T3nK8D7wengCT_A9jVIbZGSoVm9R4UDz/view
